title: Weak password storage
brief: 17:15. A copy of the customer table has appeared on a forum. Security asks how the passwords in it were stored, and how bad that is.
role: Platform engineer, reviewing a change on the Veltrix engineering team
insight: A fast hash with no salt can be reversed in minutes, and identical passwords show up as identical hashes.
teaches: Passwords need a slow, salted hash built for the job: argon2id or bcrypt
A fast general purpose hash, even a newer one, is the wrong tool
A single shared salt in the code does not stop a dictionary attack; migrate existing users on their next sign in

value.title: Password storage review
value.intro: You have the leaked table. Look at the hashes, then try to turn them back into passwords, offline, the way an attacker would.

attempts.label: Group the hashes in the dump
attempts.response:
9,812   5f4dcc3b5aa765d61d8327deb882cf99
  4,107   e10adc3949ba59abbe56e057f20f883e
  2,890   25d55ad283aa400af464c76d713c07ad

One hash appears 9,812 times. There is no salt, so the same password gives the same hash for everyone.
attempts.fixedResponse: Every stored value is different, even for the same password.

attempts.label: Run a common password list against the dump, offline
attempts.response:
Cracked 32,014 of 41,000 (78%) in 4 minutes on one graphics card.

MD5 is built to be fast. That is the problem.
attempts.fixedResponse: Estimated time to crack 1% of the dump: years. Each guess costs real time and memory.

fix.prompt: Pick every change that makes stolen hashes expensive to crack, and moves the users you already have.

options.label: Hash with argon2id (or bcrypt), with a random salt per user
code: + return argon2id.hash(plain, { memory: 64 * 1024, iterations: 3 });   // salt included and unique
options.why: Slow on purpose, memory hungry, and every user gets a different salt, so nothing can be cracked in bulk.

options.label: Upgrade existing users: verify with the old hash, then re-hash on their next sign in
code: + if (looksLikeMd5(stored) && md5(plain) === stored) { save(user, storePassword(plain)); return true; }
options.why: Nobody is locked out, and old hashes disappear as people sign in. You can also wrap the old hashes in the new one straight away.

options.label: Switch from MD5 to SHA-256
options.why: Still a fast hash. A graphics card tries billions of SHA-256 guesses a second. Only the slow, salted functions work.

options.label: Add one secret string to every password before hashing
options.why: One shared salt still gives identical hashes for identical passwords, and once it leaks (it is in the code) the whole table is open again.

options.label: Require 12 character passwords from now on
options.why: A good policy, but it does not change how the ones already stolen are stored.

outcome.label: Read the vulnerable code first
outcome.what: Reading the code before attacking it tells you where to look, and why it fails.
outcome.ideal: reads the code under review before trying to break it.

outcome.label: Tried normal use first
outcome.what: Knowing what a good request looks like is how you spot a bad one.
outcome.ideal: establishes normal behaviour before testing the abnormal.

outcome.label: Checked normal use still works
outcome.what: A fix that breaks real users gets reverted, and the bug comes back.
outcome.ideal: tests that the fix did not break normal use.

outcome.label: Reproduced the bug
outcome.what: MD5 with no salt means one guess tests every user at once, and it runs at billions per second. The most common password appears 9,812 times, all with the same hash.
outcome.ideal: proves a bug is real before fixing it.

card.title: 78% of the table, in four minutes
body: MD5 with no salt means one guess tests every user at once, and it runs at billions per second. The most common password appears 9,812 times, all with the same hash.
The leak itself was bad. The storage made it far worse.
card.ideal: reproduces a bug first, so the fix can be proved to work.

fix.objective: Fix it: pick the changes on the Fix tab that close the hole for good, then apply the patch.

label: Picked everything that fixes it? Apply the patch
Pick every change that fixes the cause
Open the Fix tab

hint.text: Pick every change that removes the cause. Avoid changes an attacker can walk around, and ones that do not touch the problem. Then Apply the patch.

outcome.label: Applied a real fix
outcome.what: Argon2id is deliberately slow and memory hungry, and each user gets their own random salt, so an attacker must attack one account at a time at real cost. Re-hashing at sign in moves your existing users without locking anyone out.
outcome.ideal: fixes the cause, not the symptom.

card.title: Slow, salted, and moving everyone across
body: Argon2id is deliberately slow and memory hungry, and each user gets their own random salt, so an attacker must attack one account at a time at real cost. Re-hashing at sign in moves your existing users without locking anyone out.
Store passwords so that a stolen table is a problem for the attacker.
card.ideal: fixes the cause with the standard control, and adds defence in depth.

outcome.label: Applied a fix that can be bypassed
outcome.what: SHA-256 is another fast hash, and one global salt in the code is a secret an attacker gets with the code. Both still fall to a wordlist in minutes.
outcome.ideal: fixes the cause instead of blocking one payload or hiding the symptom.

card.title: Still fast, still crackable
body: SHA-256 is another fast hash, and one global salt in the code is a secret an attacker gets with the code. Both still fall to a wordlist in minutes.
The property that matters is slowness, per user, on purpose.
card.ideal: fixes the cause, and knows why a blocklist or a hidden field is not a fix.

outcome.label: Applied a patch that was not enough
outcome.what: The patch missed part of the fix, or added a change that does not address the problem.

card.title: Not enough
body: The patch missed something that has to change, or included a change that does nothing for this bug. Open the Fix tab to see which options were right, missed, or wrong, and why.
A partial fix is the most dangerous kind: everyone assumes it is closed.

verify.objective: Prove it: re-run the exploit on the Exploit tab, then check normal use still works.

label: Send the exploit again: it should be blocked
Open the Exploit tab

hint.text: On the Exploit tab, send the exploit again. It should be blocked. Then send the normal request to check nothing broke.

outcome.label: Proved the exploit is blocked
outcome.what: The same request that worked before now fails, and normal use still works.
outcome.ideal: verifies a fix by re-running the exploit.

card.title: Fixed, and proved
body: You re-ran the exact request that broke it, and it is blocked. A fix you have not tested against the exploit is a hope, not a fix.
Add the exploit as an automated test so nobody can quietly bring the bug back.
card.ideal: turns the exploit into a regression test.

outcome.label: The exploit still works
outcome.what: The patch did not close the hole. The same kind of request still gets through.
outcome.ideal: never ships a fix without re-running the exploit.

card.title: Still open
body: The exploit still works after your patch. This is what happens when a fix blocks one payload, or hides a symptom, instead of removing the cause.
Go back over the Fix tab: it shows which options were right, and why the others fail.
card.ideal: verifies with the exploit before calling it fixed.
